cases.rule: Diverticular Disease Rule: IL-6i (e.g., TCZ) & JAKi risk diverticulitis/perforation. Use alternatives first.
cases.vignette:
A 60-year-old woman with known seropositive CCP-positive rheumatoid arthritis presents to clinic for follow-up. She is currently on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and sulfasalazine 1.5 grams BD and has been so for the last 6 months. Her other comorbidities include hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and previous bowel surgery secondary to diverticulitis five years ago.

Currently, she has 15 tender joints and 8 swollen joints. Her DAS28 CRP is 6.4 and DAS28-ESR is 6.2. She is counselled on commencing biologic therapy which she is agreeable to. A pre-biologic screen is entirely normal.
cases.question: Which biologic therapy should be avoided in this patient?
cases.explanation:
All of the above biologic therapies are licensed for use in rheumatoid arthritis. Selection of a biologic therapy should always involve discussion with the patient and should take into account the patient’s comorbidities and other medication. Where possible, an MDT decision can often support selection.

This patient has active rheumatoid arthritis. She qualifies for biologic therapy based on NICE criteria. Because of her background of diverticular disease, an IL-6 inhibitor such as tocilizumab is best avoided as it may increase the risk of recurrence of diverticulitis, which can then lead to other complications such as bowel perforation. Diverticular disease, however, is not an absolute contraindication, so tocilizumab could still be considered, for example, if all other possible biologic therapies fail. In this patient’s case, this does not apply.

JAK inhibitors also have a similar caution regarding diverticular disease.
resources: Medicines.org.uk (updated Nov 2019). RoActemra 162 mg solution for injection in pre-filled syringe. Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) - (emc).

NICE (2016). Technology appraisal guidance [TA375]: Adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab pegol, golimumab, tocilizumab and abatacept for rheumatoid arthritis not previously treated with DMARDs or after conventional DMARDs only have failed.

cases.question: What is the ideal disease-modifying drug for this patient?

choices.text: Start on hydroxychloroquine at 400 mg/day and methotrexate at 10 mg per week
Start on methotrexate at 15 mg per week
Start on prednisolone only at 10 mg/day
Start on sulfasalazine at 1g/day and titrate the dose

cases.explanation: This patient has active rheumatoid arthritis (RA) with co-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD) [(stage 4 - creatinine clearance (15-30 ml/min)]. Among the available options, leflunomide is the ideal drug with nil renal excretion. It can be used without any dose modification in all stages of CKD except stage V (due to a lack of data on end-stage renal disease). Sulfasalazine has 10-15% renal excretion and can be used in CKD stages I-III. In stages IV and V, it has to be started at a lower dose with caution. This patient is allergic to sulfa drugs, so it cannot be used. Hydroxychloroquine needs dose adjustments in stage III (75% of the dose) and stage IV/V (25-50% of the dose). Methotrexate needs dose adjustment (50-100%, maximum of 15 mg/week) in stage III, and is contraindicated in stage IV and V CKD. Hence, methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine are not ideal in this patient with active RA and stage IV CKD.
resources: Harty T, O'Shaughnessy M, Harney S. Therapeutics in rheumatology and the kidney. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2023 Mar 1;62(3):1009-1020. doi: 10.1093/rheumatology/keac460. PMID: 35951751.

cases.rule: US in RA Rule: RA shows hypoechoic synovitis with PDUS hyperaemia and marginal erosions (classically 2nd/5th MCP, 5th MTP, distal ulna), unlike the central erosions in OA.
cases.vignette:
A 70-year-old woman comes to the rheumatology outpatient department with a 1-year history of early morning stiffness lasting for 20-25 minutes and pain in both finger joints, especially the PIP joints.

On examination, you find minimal puffiness of the fingers bilaterally without any appreciable synovitis. You could palpate some Heberden and Bouchard nodes. At this point, you do not have access to the patient's baseline immunological investigations, so you decide to perform a bedside ultrasound scan to assess for inflammation. She does complain of mechanical pain in her knees but is otherwise pain-free in her other joints.

The ultrasound images of MCP joints can be seen below:
cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is rheumatoid arthritis. The question tests the interpretation of ultrasound findings in such patients and highlights the importance of a bedside ultrasound scan in detecting inflammation, which is critical for starting therapy. Although there is a background presence of osteoarthritis, and although it might be tempting to label it as osteoarthritis given the clinical picture, the presence of synovitis and typical marginal erosion (as pointed out by the thick and thin grey arrows, respectively) are classical of rheumatoid arthritis. Ultrasonography in the (a) longitudinal and (b) transverse planes show signs of destruction (grade 2). Synovial hypertrophy is seen as poorly compressible, hypoechoic (relative to subdermal fat) intracapsular structure (i.e., seen within the joint capsule on grayscale (GS) image), whereas active inflammation can be seen as increased signals (red spot) suggestive of hyperaemia seen on power doppler ultrasound (PDUS). It should be noted that fluid in the joint is anechoic without any signals on PDUS. The severity of synovitis is determined by a scoring system proposed by EULAR/OMERACT task force, wherein grade 0 to 3 stands for normal, mild, moderate, and severe synovitis respectively (using both GS and PD images).

Although the presence of bone erosions was classically thought to be specific for RA, it can be found in quite a lot of osteoarthritis cases. The location and size, particularly larger erosions at the second and fifth metacarpophalangeal joints, fifth metatarsophalangeal joint, and distal ulna, may point towards RA. Bone erosion in RA is typically marginal while it is central in osteoarthritis.
resources: Kaeley, G.S., Bakewell, C. & Deodhar, A. The importance of ultrasound in identifying and differentiating patients with early inflammatory arthritis: a narrative review. Arthritis Res Ther 22, 1 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1186/s13075-019-2050-4.

cases.rule: Start anti-TNF if ≥3 swollen and ≥3 tender joints (dactylitis = 1) after failing ≥2 DMARDs. Record baseline global assessments and PASI.
cases.vignette:
A 36-year-old gentleman with psoriatic arthritis for 10 years attends rheumatology outpatients for follow-up. He currently takes subcutaneous methotrexate 25mg weekly, having previously been intolerant of oral methotrexate due to nausea. 5 years ago he failed to improve after taking sulfasalazine for 9 months. He was seen 1 month ago by the rheumatology clinical nurse specialist, who found swelling and tenderness in his right knee, left ankle, and both wrists.

He currently reports pain and swelling of his left ankle, right knee, both wrists, right index finger and left little finger. Clinical examination confirms synovitis and tenderness of these joints.
cases.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
cases.explanation: This gentleman meets BSR criteria for anti-TNF therapy with greater than three swollen joints and greater than three tender joints. Dactylitis counts as one joint. Before initiation of anti-TNF therapy, it is also recommended that baseline readings for patient and physician global assessments (Likert scales 0-5), tender and swollen joint counts and PASI (Psoriasis Area Severity Index) are recorded.
resources: Kyle S. et al (2005) Guideline for anti-TNFa therapy in psoriatic arthritis. Rheumatology 44: 390-397.

cases.rule: GPA Induction Rule: Use IV pulsed CYC + oral steroids for severe/sight-threatening GPA. Diagnosis requires ≥2 ACR criteria: nasal/oral signs, CXR nodules, microhaematuria, or granulomatous biopsy.
cases.vignette:
A 56-year-old woman is referred to the clinic with a two-month history of deteriorating and painful left-sided eye protrusion. She also described joint pains, a 3 kg unintentional weight loss and irritating cough. On further questioning, she was aware of some nasal crusting and discharge.

On examination, there was left-sided exophthalmos associated with some lateral gaze diplopia. Pulse was 85 bpm and blood pressure 132/88 mmHg.

Of note in the blood tests, U+Es were normal, urinalysis was normal and proteinase 3 and ANCA were positive. CT of the orbits revealed a pseudotumour of the left orbit.
cases.question: What would be the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

choices.text: Pulsed cyclophosphamide fortnightly plus oral glucocorticoids
Pulsed IV prednisolone followed by oral prednisolone

cases.explanation: This patient has Wegener’s (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) as suggested by the arthritis, nasal involvement and pseudotumour of the left orbit. According to the American College of Rheumatology, criteria for the diagnosis of GPA include (1) nasal or oral inflammation, (2) respiratory radiographic abnormalities consistent with respiratory tissue destruction (e.g. nodules, infiltrates and cavities), (3) microhematuria or red blood cell casts on urinary sediment analysis and (4) granulomatous inflammation on biopsy for pathology. There is a roughly 90% sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis when two of the four criteria are met. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody serologies for cytoplasmic ANCA reactive against proteinase 3, as well as perinuclear ANCA reactive against myeloperoxidase, are highly useful in GPA diagnosis with positive cANCA being highly specific and sensitive. The most appropriate approach to treatment is with IV pulsed cyclophosphamide together with oral steroids, which is successful in 90% of cases with roughly 75% achieving disease remission. Rituximab is also an option but can be slower-acting.
resources: Muller, K. and Lin, J. H. (2014). Orbital granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis): clinical and pathologic findings. Archives of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, 138(8), pp. 1110–1114.

cases.rule: Early RA Rule: Start MTX monotherapy + bridging steroids (even if severe/erosive). Biologics require failing 2 DMARDs (6 months each). Prioritize tight monitoring and treat-to-target.
cases.vignette:
A 32-year-old woman presents with severe synovitis of PIPs, MCPs, wrists, left shoulder and knee and MTPs. She has a family history of rheumatoid arthritis in both her mother and maternal aunt. Her GP has already arranged investigations which reveal:

Her DAS 28 is as follows:

On x-ray, there are erosions of the 3rd and 4th MTPs.
cases.question: With which of the following would you commence therapy?
cases.explanation: The guidance has recently changed where combination therapy was considered the best approach for moderate-to-severe onset RA (ie. seropositive, erosive at presentation, high inflammatory markers at presentation)and now monotherapy, especially with Methotrexate as first-line, is advocated. Steroids are certainly implicated in this scenario to gain prompt control while awaiting the response to the methotrexate. Tight monitoring of disease and rapid alteration of therapy according to the DAS score in the first year of care seemed to be more important than the combination of DMARDs used. With this in mind, NICE guidance recommends a step-down approach rather than a step-up approach to early treatment with DMARDs meaning that it is more important to treat early and aggressively, where possible than to switch through several DMARD monotherapies hoping to achieve control. According to NICE guidance unless a patient has undergone trials of two disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), including methotrexate (unless contraindicated) biologic therapies should not be given. A trial of a DMARD is defined as being normally 6 months, with 2 months at standard dose unless significant toxicity has limited the dose or duration of treatment.
resources: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management (2018) NICE guideline NG100.

cases.rule: Seronegative RA Rule: High urate is a "red herring." Symmetric polyarthritis + US synovitis (without tophi/double-contour sign) = Seronegative RA

cases.rule: Gout Microscopy Rule: Urate: Needle-shaped & negatively birefringent (Yellow = Parallel/East-West; Blue = Perpendicular/North-South). CPPD: Rhomboid & positively birefringent.
cases.vignette:
An 80-year-old man presents to the emergency department with an erythematous, swollen left knee. He has a past medical history of hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and recurrent urinary tract infections. His temp is 37.8°C. His bloods are:

A joint aspirate is shown below:
cases.question: What is the diagnosis?
cases.explanation: The microscopy shows needle-shaped crystals, which are typical of gout. Urate crystals have a negative birefringence to polarised light, and this depends on the direction the crystals are facing (note that the north-south crystals are blue; east-west crystals are yellow). Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are rhomboid. Hydroxyapatite crystals are not seen under conventional microscopy.

cases.rule: Pregnancy DMARD Rule: Switch MTX to Sulfasalazine (safe + 5mg folic acid) at least 4 weeks pre-conception; Hydroxychloroquine is safe but less potent, while Tocilizumab requires a 3-month washout.
cases.vignette:
A 35-year-old woman, who has known rheumatoid arthritis, informs you that she wishes to become pregnant. She was diagnosed 3 years ago and has been in remission for the last 15 months. The patient’s Disease Activity Score 28 (DAS28) CRP in the clinic today is 0.8. Currently, she is on methotrexate 17.5 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg weekly, and a Vitamin E supplement, which she buys over the counter for hair loss. She was discontinued on hydroxychloroquine previously as it caused troublesome skin patches, which took many months to fully clear.

She informs you that she is very concerned about a flare of her arthritis as well as her medication harming the baby. She is very keen not to change her medications as it has taken a long time for her to achieve remission unless it harms the baby. She has two kids who are 5 and 7 years of age, respectively.
cases.question: What is the recommended treatment plan for this patient?

choices.text: Continue methotrexate and omit once the pregnancy is confirmed and start on sulfasalazine
Omit methotrexate for at least 4 weeks in advance and restart her on hydroxychloroquine
Omit methotrexate for at least 4 weeks in advance and start her on low dose prednisolone and vitamin D
Omit methotrexate for at least 4 weeks in advance and start her on sulfasalazine with supplementary folic acid
Omit methotrexate for at least 4 weeks in advance and start her on tocilizumab

cases.explanation:
Planning pregnancy for patients on DMARDs can be tricky. The disease remission should be maintained and the patient must be on medications that are proven safe for the foetus. The guidance for prescribing DMARDs in pregnancy is mentioned in the 2016 BSR and BHPR guidelines on prescribing drugs in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy and should be at least 4 weeks in advance to avoid the fetotoxic effects. Although hydroxychloroquine is safe in pregnancy, this is not an ideal option as this patient already had a dermatological issue which took months to settle. On the other hand, it will not have the potency to replace the effect of such a dose of methotrexate. Sulfasalazine is safe in pregnancy (with 5 mg of folic acid) and will be the best option for her. Tocilizumab should be stopped 3 months in advance as it is not deemed to be safe during pregnancy.
resources: Flint, J Panchal, S Hurrell, A et al, (2016), BSR and BHPR guideline on prescribing drugs in pregnancy and breastfeeding—Part I: standard and biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs and corticosteroids, Rheumatology, Volume 55, Issue 9, Pages 1693–1697

cases.rule: Leflunomide Pregnancy Rule: Perform washout with Cholestyramine 8g TDS for 11 days; confirm levels are <0.02 mg/L on two separate tests (at least 14 days apart) before conceiving.
cases.vignette: A 28-year-old woman is on 10mg leflunomide OD for rheumatoid arthritis and approaches you with plans to get pregnant.
cases.question: What would you advise?

choices.text: Cholestyramine 8g TDS washout for 11 days and leflunomide levels must be checked twice before trying to conceive
Cholestyramine 8g TDS washout for 11 days and wait for 2 weeks after this before trying to conceive
Stop leflunomide for 3 months prior to trying to conceive
Stop leflunomide for 6 months prior to conceiving
This patient should not try conceiving for at least 2 years prior to stopping leflunomide

cases.explanation: According to the summary of product characteristics, following the washout procedures, verification by 2 separate tests at an interval of at least 14 days and a waiting period of one-and-a-half months between the first occurrence of a plasma concentration below 0.02 mg/L and fertilisation is required.
resources: Arava, INN-leflunomide. Summary of Product Characteristics

cases.rule: Rheumatoid Vasculitis Rule: Chronic, "burnt-out" RA (wrist ankylosis, MCP erosions, DIP sparing) plus systemic signs (foot drop/mononeuritis, leg ulcers, nail fold infarcts) indicates Rheumatoid Vasculitis, a severe extra-articular complication often linked to smoking and untreated disease.
cases.vignette:
A 70-year-old woman has had a leg ulcer on her left leg for a month which has not healed despite antibiotics prescribed by her general practitioner (GP). She is now admitted to the Acute Medicine Unit after tripping over and falling in her bathroom, and the Acute Medical doctors noted that she had a right foot drop which probably contributed to her fall.

Her only past medical history, according to her son, is an arthritic disease, diagnosed about 15 years ago when she was given some medications. However, she had stopped taking her medications after a few months due to gastric intolerance. She is currently only taking doxycycline prescribed by her GP. She also has a 20-pack-year smoking history.

The Acute Medicine consultant requests an opinion from you, the on-call Rheumatologist, to diagnose her underlying arthritic disease and has, helpfully, already done an X-ray of her left hand with the most severe deformities.

On examination, the patient is alert but confused, with a temperature of 38oC, a pulse rate of 110/min, blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg and a respiratory rate of 21/min.

Bilateral nail fold infarcts are noted. A right foot drop is noted. The patient’s left eye is congested and oedematous. A punched-out 7cm ulcer is noted over the left medial malleolus with surrounding erythema.

A cardiorespiratory examination is unremarkable.

Musculoskeletal examination: Severe muscle wasting of both hands and feet along with deformities noted. No active synovial inflammation is noted.

Her left-hand X-ray is shown below:
cases.question: What is the likely underlying arthritic disease in this patient?

choices.text: Systemic lupus erythaematosus with Jaccoud’s arthropathy

cases.explanation:
(Distal interphalangeal -DIP, Proximal interphalangeal -PIP, Metacarpophalangeal – MCP, CMC- carpometacarpal)

The hand X-rays show severe osteopenia, volar subluxation at the wrist ( lateral view), severe carpal /wrist ankylosis, a Boutonniere deformity(Flexed PIP, extended DIP), erosive disease of the metacarpal base and heads, erosions and dislocation of the 2nd MCP joint, 3rd -5th MCP joint and PIP arthritides with symmetric joint space loss, subluxation of the 1st CMC joint and Nalebuff Type-3 rheumatoid thumb deformity (swan neck thumb deformity) with sparing of the DIP joints, all consistent with chronic established rheumatoid arthritis.

Image source: Author.

Red circle: severe carpal /wrist ankylosis

Green arrow: subluxation of the 1st CMC joint

Pink arrows: Nalebuff Type- 3 rheumatoid thumb deformity ( swan neck thumb deformity)

Yellow arrow: erosions and dislocation of the 2nd MCP joint

Black rectangle: erosive disease of the metacarpal heads, 2nd -5th MCP arthritis

Blue rectangles: PIP erosive arthritis

Purple arrows: Relatively preserved DIP joints

The image next to the annotated hand -x ray is an x-ray of a normal hand for comparison; not only is there gross erosive disease of the patient’s hand evident, but the diffuse osteopenia can also be appreciated when compared.

Image source: Author

Red rectangle: volar subluxation at the wrist

Blue rectangle: a Boutonniere deformity( Flexed PIP, extended DIP)

This patient’s clinical presentation with acute mononeuritis, possible scleritis, digital nail fold infarcts, constitutional symptoms, non-healing leg ulcer, features of ‘burnt-out’ rheumatoid arthritis with deformities which has been untreated for 14-15 years with typical deformities all point to a diagnosis of rheumatoid vasculitis(RV). Her smoking history also increases her risk for RV.

Gouty arthritis can be associated with punched-out erosions (mouse-bitten) with sclerotic overhanging edges but usually preserved joint space until very late.

Jaccoud arthropathy is characterised by lax deformities of the joints which are voluntarily correctable by patients without erosive articular disease in the X-rays. It is usually associated with recurrent rheumatic fever but is also seen in patients with SLE (5%) and occasionally in other auto-immune diseases.

Erosive osteoarthritis is unlikely given the severe erosive disease, wrist ankylosis and sparing of DIP in this patient.

Arthritis mutilans, which is a severe deforming and destructive arthritis, is seen in about 5% of patients with psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and is characterised by osteolysis of the bone and marked destruction of the digits with shortening. The typical erosive RA appearance with DIP sparing in this patient is against PsA and the evolution into current acute vasculitis also is consistent with rheumatoid arthritis.

cases.rule: PsA Management Rule: For axial PsA with extensive skin disease, Secukinumab (IL-17i) is preferred over TNF inhibitors for superior skin efficacy; MTX/SSZ are ineffective for axial symptoms.
cases.vignette:
A 39-year-old man presented to your clinic with a two-year history of intermittent low back pain, which was experienced in the early morning on waking. At times, the pain was severe enough that it disturbed his sleep. The patient advised that the pain eased after 1 hour of being awake. He described a history of pain and swelling in multiple joints of his upper and lower limbs and skin psoriasis for the past 5 years, for which he was on topical medications. There was a recent worsening of the skin lesions.

On examination he had swelling and tenderness of the right ankle and left wrist. He had extensive psoriatic lesions over his scalp, trunk and both lower limbs. He was started on etoricoxib 90 mg once daily, apremilast (titrated to 30 mg twice daily) with methotrexate 10 mg per week. After 12 weeks of review, he felt symptomatically better with a reduction of pain in the peripheral joints. However, he continued to have active skin lesions and severe low back pain with morning stiffness and fatigue.

His follow-up investigations taken at 12 weeks are mentioned below:
workup: Sclerosis, erosions with widening of right sacroiliac joint
cases.question: What would be the preferred option for further management?

choices.text: Step up the dose of methotrexate

cases.explanation: This patient has severe skin psoriasis with axial and peripheral joint involvement. The peripheral arthritis improved with apremilast and methotrexate. For patients with predominant axial symptoms with extensive skin involvement, biologics may be considered, provided there is an inadequate response of axial symptoms to NSAIDs. Among the biologics, IL-17 inhibitor may be preferred in comparison to TNF inhibitor considering its greater efficacy for skin involvement. If there is concomitant uveitis or bowel inflammation, TNF inhibitors (except etanercept) are preferred. Methotrexate and intra-articular steroids may not be useful in axial disease, though methotrexate may help for cutaneous psoriasis. The liver enzymes are also mildly raised in this patient, so stepping up methotrexate is difficult. Tofacitinib has been approved for psoriatic arthritis but not for cutaneous psoriasis. Sulfasalazine is not effective for cutaneous psoriasis or axial involvement in psoriatic arthritis. So the best option here will be the IL-17 inhibitor Secukinumab.

EULAR recommendations for the management of psoriatic arthritis with pharmacological therapies: 2019 update. Annals of the rheumatic diseases, 79(6), pp.700-712.

cases.rule: Demyelination Rule: Stop Anti-TNFs (e.g., Adalimumab) if demyelination occurs; switch to a non-TNF biologic like Sarilumab (IL-6i) or a tsDMARD, as Anti-TNFs are contraindicated.
cases.vignette:
A 45-year-old woman was referred to you from the neurology clinic for further assessment of her therapy. She was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis two years ago and was previously on methotrexate and leflunomide. Despite that, her DAS 28 CRP score was more than 6.0 in two separate assessments and subcutaneous adalimumab was started six months back. cases.vignette: A 55-year-old man presents to you in clinic with recurrent aspirate-proven gout, namely of the feet, ankles and knees. His serum urate is 600 µmol/L. He also suffers from hypertension and has a BMI of 40 kg/m2. You provide lifestyle advice and initiate allopurinol with colchicine. He asks you about specific dietary measures which can help reduce his urate levels.
cases.question: Which of the following food and drink products may help reduce serum urate levels?
cases.explanation:
Apart from medication, addressing lifestyle factors such as diet, alcohol intake, weight control and exercise are all important in the management of chronic gout. Various food and drink products may either increase or decrease serum urate levels.

Encouraging patients to have a low-purine diet is imperative. Thus they should avoid or minimise consumption of seafood and red meat. Alcohol, fructose-rich fruit juices and soda should similarly be avoided as they also stimulate uric acid production. On the contrary, purine-rich vegetables such as spinach, lentils and peas show mixed results in studies (i.e. stimulating hyperuricaemia, having no effect or stimulating hypouricaemia) – overall they should be encouraged as a substitute to meat products given their overall benefit towards weight loss, and the cardiovascular and gastrointestinal systems.

The BSR specifically recommends cherries as they appear to have uricosuric properties and thus help reduce serum urate. Other vitamin C-rich products, soybeans, low-fat yoghurt and semi-skimmed milk may also help.

She has a medical history of myopia and cleft palate. On examination, she was noted to wear hearing aids. She had scoliosis and was hypermobile. She had crepitus on examination of her joints, but no obvious effusion. ANA, RF and ACPA were negative. Full blood count, renal function and liver function were unremarkable. CRP was within a normal range.
cases.question: What is the diagnosis?
cases.explanation: This patient presents with early-onset osteoarthritis. Although secondary causes of this include inflammatory arthritis, a combination of myopia, cleft palate, hearing loss and scoliosis, the absence of any immunological markers makes Stickler syndrome the most likely diagnosis. She is hypermobile, but there is nothing in the history or examination to suggest classical Ehlers–Danlos syndrome.

cases.explanation: Fluffy periostitis and ankylosis are highly characteristic of psoriatic arthritis, especially in axial or mutilans forms. Erosive changes typically co-exist with new bone formation. Marginal erosions, symmetrical joint space narrowing and periarticular osteopenia are more typical of rheumatoid arthritis. Central erosions in the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints are a key feature of erosive osteoarthritis.
